blocks.text:
Before prioritizing four to six servings of whole grains every day, it’s important to understand that the study comes with some caveats.

For one, researchers measured changes in risk factors, not whether people actually avoided heart attacks, strokes, or death. Improvements in cholesterol or blood pressure are meaningful, but they’re still a step removed from proving that whole grains directly prevent disease.

Some of the improvements were also modest, and the strength of the evidence wasn’t uniform. The researchers rated their confidence as high for some outcomes, such as total cholesterol and body weight, but lower for others.

Additionally, most of the included trials were relatively short, with an average duration of about eight weeks, Helda Tutunchi, PhD, an associate professor of nutritional sciences at Tabriz University of Medical Sciences in Iran, wrote in a press release. “As a result, we cannot determine whether these benefits are maintained over the long term,” she said.3

And relatively few studies evaluated very high whole-grain intakes, above 140 grams per day, so the effects at those intake levels remain uncertain, Tutunchi added.

The study should not be treated as a recommendation to start eating four to six servings of whole grains every day, according to ⟦1⟧, a Florida-based registered dietitian.

She said the study suggests that about four to six servings of whole grains a day may give the strongest heart-health benefits. But people do not need to reach that number overnight if it is not already part of their eating habits.

For most people,” McIntyre added, “the best approach is to start where you are, make more grain choices whole grain when possible, and build toward that range over time in a way that feels realistic and sustainable.

If you already have heart disease, high cholesterol, or another cardiometabolic condition, whole grains can be one helpful part of your eating plan. But they are not a replacement for prescribed medicine or your doctor’s advice.

blocks.title: Talk with your care team
blocks.text: Talk with your care team before making big diet changes, especially if you take medicines that affect blood sugar or blood pressure, since diet changes can affect your treatment.

items.title: What we’re talking about
items.text: A new study suggests that eating four to six servings of whole grains a day may offer the greatest heart-health benefits.

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Dietary guidelines in the United States recommend aiming for just two to four servings of whole grains a day.

items.title: What you can do
items.text: Instead of trying to reach four to six servings overnight, prioritize whole grains over refined grains when possible and gradually increase your intake.

blocks.text:
You may already know that whole grains are good for your heart. That message has been a staple of nutrition advice for decades. What’s been less clear is exactly how much you need to eat to see the benefits—and whether more is always better.

A new European study helps answer those questions. Published in the European Heart Journal, the analysis suggests that eating around four to six servings of whole grains a day may be the sweet spot for improving several markers of heart health. That’s slightly more than the average of three daily servings recommended under current ⟦1⟧.12

So should you aim to add more brown rice and whole-grain bread to your plate? We’ve got you covered.

The researchers pooled data from 87 randomized controlled trials, which are considered the strongest type of study for cause and effect. Instead of just asking whether whole grains help, they looked at how the amount people ate matched the size of the benefit. That is something research has often skipped.

items.meaning: Studies that compare groups in a fair way to see what causes what.
Health of the heart, blood vessels, blood sugar, and related risks.

blocks.text: Across the trials, eating more whole grains was linked to better scores on several heart and blood vessel risk factors. These included LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, total cholesterol, triglycerides, blood pressure, fasting blood sugar, markers of ⟦1⟧, and things like body weight and waist size.

rows.label: Most benefits
rows.value: about 60 to 100 grams of whole grains per day by dry weight

rows.label: Prepared food
rows.value: about 115 to 190 grams, or about four to six servings

rows.label: One serving
rows.value: about a slice of whole-grain bread, a half-cup of cooked oatmeal or brown rice, or a small bowl of whole-grain cereal

rows.label: Guideline range
rows.value: two to four servings of whole grains per day, depending on individual calorie needs

blocks.text: Whole grains have long been recommended in a healthy diet because, unlike refined grains, they keep all parts of the seed kernel, which is rich in fiber and other nutrients, according to ⟦2⟧, a cardiologist and author of The 5CH Lifestyle, a book about how to lower your cholesterol. Fiber can also slow digestion, improve blood sugar control, and help lower LDL cholesterol, all of which can help cardiometabolic health.
